I am often asked why rotations happen instead of managers simply going to cash.  The answer lies within investment mandates.  Many managers have to stay long equities with most of their AUM.  That means they can't just sell down the entire portfolio and raise cash.  But, many mandates afford some flexibility. As a result, when managers become more defensive they're likely to rotate instead of just selling.  Meaning you'll see them switch their asset allocation preferences to parts of the market that are lower beta, often in areas that pay dividends.  Examples include utilities, healthcare and consumer staples.  That's why on a day where the market leadership is red and even the indices are red you may see patches of green in the more defensive sectors and industries.  Often is the case that managed money is rotating their long equity exposure to be more defensive so as to minimize losses.  That's why rotations tend to happen and also why they can offer us, as smaller traders and investors, potential opportunities.  If you are a large asset manager you can't rotate your portfolio to be more defensive in a day or even a week. It can take quite a lot of time.  While that hand-off is happening there is typically weakness in high beta stocks and strength in low beta high-dividend payers.  This sets up pair trades, like long $SPHD and short $SPHB (equal size, re-balanced weekly) to benefit from the risk-off rotation.  And that concludes my Ted Talk on rotations. I hope you learned something new today! :-)

The death of the average.  We are currently witnessing the total collapse of the marginal cost of creation. Copywriting, design, video editing - skills that previously commanded a premium due to the barrier of technical execution are being democratised to the point of irrelevance.  Most marketers view this through the lens of efficiency. They see a tool that allows them to produce 10x the output for 1/10th of the cost.  When the supply of "good enough" content becomes infinite, the economic value of that content plummets to zero. We are entering an era of infinite noise. If you think it is hard to capture attention now, wait until the internet is flooded with billions of synthetically generated articles, tweets, and videos every single day.  (Which is already happening, just not at the quality and volume that it will in 6, 12 months from now)  In this environment, pure volume is no longer a valid strategy. You cannot out-publish a server farm.  The alpha in modern marketing is shifting entirely from production to provenance.  [1] The Trust Premium  As the internet becomes increasingly synthetic, we will see a massive flight to safety. "Is this real?" will become the single most important buying criterion.  We are moving away from algorithm-optimisation and back towards human-optimisation. Personal brands, founders-led sales, and verified human voices will command an exorbitant premium.  The faceless corporate brand is dead. If a consumer cannot verify the human source behind the message, they will subconsciously label it as "spam".  [2] High-Friction Marketing  For the last decade, the goal was "low friction". SEO, programmatic ads, automated email sequences.  As AI cannibalises these low-friction channels, - bots clicking on ads served by bots on sites written by bots - the smart money will move to high-friction channels.  Live events. Physical mail. Handshakes. Closed-door dinners.  The harder it is to scale, the more valuable it becomes. You prove your value by doing things that cannot be automated.  [3] Taste as a Moat  Large Language Models function by predicting the next most likely token. By definition, they regress to the mean. They give you the average of the entire internet.  If you use AI to guide your strategy, you are opting for mediocrity at scale.  "Taste" - the human ability to curate, to select the outlier, to understand nuance and subtext - becomes the only defensible moat.  The future of marketing is about who has the taste to know what *not* to create.  Paradoxically, the more artificial the world becomes, the higher the premium on being undeniably human.

AI Capex Isn’t a Bubble! It’s a Prisoners’ Dilemma Arms Race.   AI capex is being misframed as a bubble when, in reality, it is a prisoners’ dilemma arms race in which firms and nations either spend or accept strategic decline, with AI capacity now inseparable from control over compute, energy, and critical inputs.  Many core AI infrastructure names, including leading chip, hardware, and data-center providers, trade on valuation metrics comparable to or, on growth-adjusted bases, cheaper than slower-growing consumer staples like large-box retailers, despite far greater structural upside from the AI buildout.  In a classic prisoners’ dilemma, each player would prefer mutual restraint, but once one defects, everyone else must follow or be dominated; that is exactly what is happening as hyperscalers, chipmakers, and platform companies commit to AI at industrial scale.  Calling this a bubble confuses forced strategic investment with optional speculative excess and ignores that the Nash equilibrium has shifted from “optimize margins” to “invest or be structurally weakened.”  This is not just a corporate contest; it is increasingly a question of national security, as governments now view AI leadership, domestic compute, and secure supply of energy and critical minerals as essential to economic resilience, information control, and defense capabilities.  Nations that under-invest in AI infrastructure, grid capacity, and upstream resources become dependent on foreign models, data centers, and materials, ceding leverage in both markets and geopolitics.  The misread is visible in equity pricing: when AI infrastructure leaders, trade on multiples lower than growth retailers. This signals that markets have not fully internalized the asymmetric payoff to scale, data, and model advantage.  One group is building the rails and power grid of the new platform while the other defends margins in the old one, yet they are often modeled as if they face the same game.  The through line is straightforward: AI capex is not discretionary, and the key AI names are not just “hot growth stocks” to fade on sentiment.  They are central players in a strategic arms race, spanning compute, energy, minerals, and infrastructure, where under-investment is tantamount to self-liquidation for both corporations and countries, and those shouting “bubble” are using yesterday’s valuation playbook for a game governed by compounding, game-theoretic positioning. Over 31% of all U.S. wealth is now held by people over 70 years old and this share has been steadily climbing since the mid 1990s.   Think of it like this, back in the 90s, people over 70 controlled roughly 20% of the nation's wealth, but that number has grown almost 60% over the past three decades.   he gray bars on the chart mark major economic disruptions like recessions, and what's interesting is that every time the economy took a hit, older Americans actually became richer relative to the rest of the population.  The 2008 financial crisis, the dot com crash, and the pandemic all show this same pattern where their share of wealth jumped or stayed resilient while everyone else got hammered.  Younger and middle aged Americans are essentially getting priced out of wealth accumulation.   When a 70 year old owns a house worth $500k that they paid $50k for in 1980, and a 35 year old is trying to buy that same house for $500k with student loans and stagnant wages, the wealth gap compounds every single year.   This isn't just about investment returns either. It's about who owns real estate, who has paid off their mortgages, and who locked in assets decades ago before prices exploded.   Meanwhile, younger generations are starting from further back, dealing with higher asset prices, and having less time to compound their wealth before they retire.  The implications are actually pretty significant for society and the market.   First, you've got potential policy risk because this creates intergenerational tension. When millennials and Gen Z realize they're essentially locked out of the wealth that older generations accumulated, you'll see pressure for taxes on capital gains, inheritance taxes, and maybe even wealth taxes.   Second, it affects consumer spending and economic growth because younger people with less wealth spend differently than older people just managing their portfolios.   Third, from a market perspective, expect shifting sector preferences as Baby Boomers gradually liquidate assets and healthcare, consumer staples, and dividend plays might outperform growth stocks.   The wealth transfer that's about to happen over the next 10-20 years will be huge but not everyone's inheriting anything, so the wealth gap might actually get worse before it gets better.

JPMorgan on "Is AI a bubble?"  Unlike past episodes of speculative excess, today’s AI cycle is being largely financed by profitable, cash-rich firms and underpinned by robust demand. The tech sector’s free cash flow margin, near 20%, is more than double its late 1990s level, underscoring both robust profitability and the capacity to self-fund AI investment. AI spending is also translating into monetized demand for AI hardware, cloud services and software, helping justify continued investment. Indeed, bubbles burst into nothing, but the AI theme is building real infrastructure to meet growing demand.   Still, markets are struggling to price a technology that is advancing at exponential speed. Earnings growth has been extraordinary, but expectations have risen even more so. Tech sectors have accounted for 36% of S&P 500 earnings and 56% of the index’s capital spending growth over the last 12 months, leaving markets vulnerable to any missteps, such as a slowdown in business adoption, power constraints or faster-than- expected hardware obsolescence. The stakes are high, and visibility into the ultimate winners limited, but this looks less like a bubble and more like the tumultuous beginnings of a structural transition.   Whether bubble or boom in valuations, profits or innovation, selectivity and balance are critical for portfolios. Within growth, the tech sectors have obvious appeal given their exemplary profits, while consumer discretionary has lagged this year, beleaguered by tariff pressures, a softening consumer and a relatively weak showing from the sector’s Mag 7 names. Within AI, beneficiaries should continue to broaden out from the innovators (tech) to the enablers (industrials, utilities) and the adopters (financials, health care). Traditional value sectors like energy and consumer staples may continue to struggle due to low oil prices and a deteriorating low- end consumer, while financials boast resilient earnings and differentiated catalysts like deregulation and yield curve steepening.   While markets appear undeterred, even with solid fundamentals markets can correct, investors should be prepared for both success and setbacks.

When gold climbs this fast, you pay attention.  The BTC-to-gold ratio dropped 50% this year and not because Bitcoin faltered.  Here’s what drove the shift and what could flip it back 👇🏻  1. Gold Takes the Lead Gold saw one of its strongest years in recent memory, climbing over 60% and briefly crossing $4,000/oz in Q4.  That move came during a year defined by high real rates and tight financial conditions, an environment where non-yielding assets typically struggle.  Instead, gold absorbed capital like a magnet. This wasn’t just sentiment.  Central banks added 254 tonnes through October, with Poland leading the way, and gold ETFs saw 397 tonnes of inflows in H1 alone: a full reversal from 2023’s outflows.  2. A Flight to Safety The appeal wasn’t only in performance.  Volatility levels rose, geopolitical risk surged, and gold’s equity beta dropped to its lowest since 2008, suggesting it served as a hedge across portfolios.  With uncertainty high and policy easing delayed until late in the year, investors leaned into gold not for yield, but for resilience.  The message: gold is still seen as the core “portfolio insurance” when macro visibility drops.  3. Bitcoin Pulls Back (Relatively) Bitcoin did well on paper, hitting six figures and gaining ETF traction, but its relative performance lagged.  After spot ETF AUM peaked near $152B in mid-2025, a slow bleed followed, with assets slipping to $112B by year-end.  Simultaneously, long-term holders offloaded over 500,000 BTC, realizing billions in profits during the summer and fall.  The drop in BTC-to-gold ratio had less to do with collapse and more with rotation.  4. Profit-Taking and Pressure By July, long-term holders were realizing $1B+ daily in profits on average.  That kind of distribution changes flows fast.  With real yields averaging near 2%, the opportunity cost of holding BTC went up.  At the same time, Bitcoin’s risk profile remained tightly correlated with equities, reducing its appeal as a defensive allocation.  Gold, on the other hand, enjoyed flows from both risk-averse and reserve-oriented buyers.  5. Ratio Compression or Reset? The drop in the BTC-to-gold ratio, from 40 to 20, reflects a repricing of short-term expectations.  But it does raise the bar for Bitcoin going into 2026.  Will Bitcoin reclaim leadership in the store-of-value rotation, or has gold set a new floor for macro trust?

I typed up my strategy on selling cash secured puts and covered calls. I follow this guide daily.  Josh’s Key Entry Rules for Selling Puts (Cash-Secured):  Only sell puts on days when the underlying stock is down (red/close lower than open or previous close).  Only sell puts on stocks I would genuinely be happy to own long-term if assigned at the chosen strike price (strong fundamentals, good balance sheet, sector I believe in).  Target a delta range of -0.16 to -0.23 (approximately 16–23 delta). This keeps the position roughly 77–84% out-of-the-money probability at entry—far enough to offer a solid edge while still collecting meaningful premium. I avoid anything higher (closer to ATM) to reduce the frequency of being tested.  Aim for 14–30 days to expiration (DTE). This sweet spot balances rapid theta decay with manageable gamma risk and gives time for the position to work.  Choose a strike price that sits below at least two clear levels of support visible on the monthly chart (e.g., prior swing lows, moving averages, trendlines, or round numbers). This adds an extra layer of technical protection against immediate downside breaches.  Additional Portfolio & Position Management Rules: Keep position sizes small (typically 1–5 contracts per trade) and spread across multiple uncorrelated sectors (e.g., tech, healthcare, consumer staples, energy). Diversification helps ensure that if one sector experiences a sharp drawdown, others may remain stable or even benefit.  For covered calls (when assigned shares from a put):  Only sell them on green/up days to capture better premiums when momentum is positive and the stock is elevated.  Exit & Risk Management Rules: Close (buy to close) both puts and covered calls when 50–70% of maximum profit has been realized. This locks in gains early, reduces exposure to late adverse moves, and frees up capital for new trades.  Always close or roll out positions well before earnings announcements to avoid unpredictable volatility spikes and gap risk.  Exit (or aggressively manage) positions ahead of major sector-specific catalysts or high-volatility events (e.g., Fed announcements impacting financials, regulatory news in biotech, or commodity shocks in energy).  By consistently applying these filters and rules—emphasizing high-probability setups, technical confluence, diversification, and disciplined profit-taking—I have found that my overall options trades end profitably more than 90% of the time over an extended sample of trades. 🚨 IF YOU TRADE THE SAME SECURITIES IN A US 🇺🇸TAXABLE AND NON-TAXABLE ACCOUNT, READ THIS!  If you sell a stock for a loss in a taxable account and buy it back in a retirement account (like an IRA or Roth IRA) within 30 days, you trigger one of the most punitive versions of the Wash Sale Rule.  This specific scenario is often called the "IRA Trap" because the tax consequences are significantly worse than a standard wash sale between two taxable accounts.  1. The Loss is Permanently Lost  In a normal wash sale (taxable to taxable), the loss is merely "deferred." The IRS doesn't let you claim the loss now, but you add it to the cost basis of the new shares. When you eventually sell those new shares, that higher basis reduces your future taxes.  However, Revenue Ruling 2008-5 states that when the replacement purchase happens in an IRA:  - The loss is disallowed in your taxable account. - You are not allowed to increase the basis of the shares in your IRA. - Result: The tax benefit of that loss disappears forever. Since retirement accounts don't track cost basis for tax purposes (withdrawals are either taxed as ordinary income or tax-free), there is no way to "recover" that loss later.  2. The 61-Day "Danger Zone"  The rule doesn't just apply to the 30 days after you sell. It covers a 61-day window:  - 30 days before the sale. - The day of the sale. - 30 days after the sale.  If you buy the stock in your IRA at any point during this window, the loss in your taxable account is wiped out.  3. Why It's Hard to Track  Your brokerage is required to track wash sales that happen within the same account. However, they generally do not track them across different accounts (like your taxable brokerage vs. your IRA) or across different institutions (e.g., selling at Fidelity and buying at Schwab).  Important: Even if your 1099-B tax form doesn't show a wash sale, the IRS still considers it one. It is your responsibility to report it correctly on your tax return (Form 8949).  How to avoid this:  If you want to keep exposure to that sector while harvesting the loss:  Wait 31 days: Wait at least 31 days before buying the same stock in your IRA.  Buy a "Similar" Asset: Buy a different stock in the same industry or an ETF that holds the stock. For example, if you sell Pepsi at a loss, you can immediately buy Coca-Cola or a Consumer Staples ETF without triggering the rule.  This is not tax advice and please consult a tax advisor.

The TLT Accumulation Story Sounds Right… Until You Zoom Out  I get why people are excited about TLT. It’s been a disaster since 2020, it’s finally stopped falling, and yields are high enough that you’re getting paid to wait. When something is that hated and it stops making new lows, the bottom is in narrative starts to feel obvious.  But the clean version of this story skips the part that matters most..why long bonds would rally from here.  What the Chart Is Really Saying  The chart mostly says we’ve moved from falling knife!to stabilizing. That’s not nothing. Bases often form when nobody wants the asset and the selling pressure just runs out of energy.  But a base isn’t the same thing as a new uptrend. Right now it’s more like..the market stopped panicking. It hasn’t started believing again.  Volume Doesn’t Automatically Mean Institutions Are Loading Up   This is where I think people get fooled.  TLT isn’t a normal investment product. It’s a macro tool. A lot of the trading is hedges, options flows, relative value trades, people rotating risk, people putting on duration as protection, then taking it off again.  So heavy volume can mean institutions are involved, sure but it doesn’t automatically mean institutions are accumulating a long.  If you want a cleaner read on accumulation, you look at flows. And lately, shares outstanding have actually been drifting lower. More people have been pulling money out than putting new money in. That’s not what quiet conviction buying looks like.  The Real Bet Here Isn’t Technical It’s Macro  The post leans on a familiar rule..when the 10 year peaks, long bonds usually rip.  That worked great in the 2010s. But we’re not in the 2010s.  Today, long rates aren’t just about growth and inflation. They’re also about supply, deficits, and term premium..the extra yield investors demand for holding long duration in a world that feels less stable.  So it’s totally possible for the Fed to ease, the front end to fall… and the long end to stay sticky because investors still want to be paid for the risk.  That’s the regime shift people keep underestimating.  What Those Price Targets Really Imply  Calling for $115–$140 sounds like sentiment turning. But it’s really a bigger claim than that.  To get a move like that, you usually need one of two things..  •   a real growth and credit shock that forces a classic flight to safety, or  •   some form of policy support that directly benefits long duration (think balance sheet tools, not just rate cuts)  Either way, the bonds rally hard because something else is breaking or the rules of the game are being changed.  So the upside is real but it’s not free.  Where This Take Could Be Wrong  If we get a genuine disinflation pulse, growth rolls over, and the market starts pricing a deeper easing cycle, TLT can absolutely rip. In that scenario, today’s prices will look like a gift.  But if the next phase is more fiscal, supply and geopolitics that’ll keep term premium elevated, then TLT might just chop sideways… or disappoint again.  That’s the fork in the road.  My View  I don’t hate TLT here. As paid insurance, it finally makes sense again. You’re earning yield while you wait, and if a real slowdown hits, you’ve got convexity.  But I wouldn’t confuse it stopped going down with it’s about to do 30–50%. That’s not a chart call. That’s a macro call.  The real question is simple..is the next shock deflationary… or is it the bond market demanding a higher price for long term risk?  Answer that, and you’ll know whether this base is a launchpad or just a pause.

This Is How Global Tightening Actually Begins  Japan spent decades trapped in nothing works territory with weak demand, falling prices, and rates pinned near zero. The BOJ became the market..not just a participant because that was the only way to keep the system from sliding back into a deflationary mindset.  Now they’re trying to exit that world without snapping the plumbing. Let yields move, let banks earn a curve, restore some honest price discovery… and, quietly, rebuild wiggle room so the next downturn isn’t fought from zero again. That’s the uncomfortable part people miss..you normalize when you can, because when the next Minsky moment arrives, you won’t get to choose the timing.  But the trade off is brutal. When the 40 year is printing 4% while the 10 year is up around 2.35%, that’s not a little normalization. That’s the market demanding real compensation for duration and reminding everyone how sensitive a high debt system is to long rates.  If U.S. and Japan yields rise together it becomes a global tightening event even without any central bank hiking.  When the two biggest safe bond markets both reprice higher at the same time..  •   The world’s discount rate resets upward (everything gets valued against it).  •   Leverage gets more expensive and less forgiving.  •   The yen carry trade starts to cough, and that’s often where stress shows up first.  •   Japanese capital has less reason to live overseas, which can mean less marginal demand for Treasuries right when the U.S. is issuing a lot.  Historically, synchronized long rate climbs don’t just go on forever. They usually end one of two ways..  1.   Something breaks and you get a real flight to safety, or  2.   Policy steps back in..directly or indirectly to put a ceiling on the long end.  Until one of those happens, rising yields together is basically the market saying that the cost of money is going up everywhere, and somebody levered is going to feel it.

I put together my strategy on selling cash secured puts and covered calls. I follow this guide daily.  Josh’s Key Entry Rules for Selling Puts (Cash-Secured):  Only sell puts on days when the underlying stock is down (red/close lower than open or previous close).  Only sell puts on stocks I would genuinely be happy to own long-term if assigned at the chosen strike price (strong fundamentals, good balance sheet, sector I believe in).  Target a delta range of -0.16 to -0.23 (approximately 16–23 delta). This keeps the position roughly 77–84% out-of-the-money probability at entry—far enough to offer a solid edge while still collecting meaningful premium. I avoid anything higher (closer to ATM) to reduce the frequency of being tested.  Aim for 14–30 days to expiration (DTE). This sweet spot balances rapid theta decay with manageable gamma risk and gives time for the position to work.  Choose a strike price that sits below at least two clear levels of support visible on the monthly chart (e.g., prior swing lows, moving averages, trendlines, or round numbers). This adds an extra layer of technical protection against immediate downside breaches.  Additional Portfolio & Position Management Rules: Keep position sizes small (typically 1–5 contracts per trade) and spread across multiple uncorrelated sectors (e.g., tech, healthcare, consumer staples, energy). Diversification helps ensure that if one sector experiences a sharp drawdown, others may remain stable or even benefit.  For covered calls (when assigned shares from a put):  Only sell them on green/up days to capture better premiums when momentum is positive and the stock is elevated.  Exit & Risk Management Rules: Close (buy to close) both puts and covered calls when 50–70% of maximum profit has been realized. This locks in gains early, reduces exposure to late adverse moves, and frees up capital for new trades.  Always close or roll out positions well before earnings announcements to avoid unpredictable volatility spikes and gap risk.  Exit (or aggressively manage) positions ahead of major sector-specific catalysts or high-volatility events (e.g., Fed announcements impacting financials, regulatory news in biotech, or commodity shocks in energy).  By consistently applying these filters and rules—emphasizing high-probability setups, technical confluence, diversification, and disciplined profit-taking—I have found that my overall options trades end profitably more than 90% of the time over an extended sample of trades. 84 million people saw 'Something Big Is Happening.' Most nodded and kept scrolling. If you actually want to do something about it: here's the financial playbook.  I told you so.. but not with joy In April 2025 I wrote: "The ease of creating new software also means existing tech products can be copied easily. They will be dismantled like a device and rebuilt by new builders who can do it leaner and cheaper and make it work better for niche segments." YTD 2026, SaaS companies have been in freefall on the markets. Not a correction, but a structural repricing. The market is finally digesting what was obvious to anyone paying attention: if a product only exists as logic on a screen and AI can rebuild that logic from scratch in days.. what exactly are you paying for? But here's what most people outside our little X bubble aren't asking: what's next after SaaS? Because this doesn't stop there.  The disruption people aren't seeing yet Everyone's focused on software eating software. That's already happening. The next wave is quieter, and hits things people consider real. Think about office real estate. Not prime, triple-A city centre locations, those adapt. I mean the B and C-grade office parks, the corporate campuses on the edge of town, the floors companies rented because headcount was growing. Remote work cracked the foundation, and now AI is pouring water into those cracks. If knowledge work becomes something one person does with AI tooling; the work of what used to be 5-10 people, you don't need the space anymore. The companies that survive will be leaner by necessity. The buildings they leave behind won't easily find new tenants, and converting them to housing is slow, expensive, and heavily dependent on local regulation and demand. Real estate moguls sitting on non-prime office assets are, in my view, in a similar position to SaaS founders in 2023. The fundamentals changed. The valuation hasn't caught up yet. This is one example. There are dozens of sectors where the same logic applies. Legal support and accountancy, some or most financial advisory. Certain medical diagnostics. Consulting layers that exist purely to synthesise information.. which is exactly what AI does for free. Nevertheless one new release: a Claude instance trained specifically on legal workflows, a model fine-tuned for a specific industry, and an entire sector faces a repricing moment. We've already seen this. It'll keep happening.  So how do you actually protect yourself over the next 5 years? First: accept that the index funds you've been told to "just hold" may not be what you think they are. A global Vanguard World ETF has always stood for being diversified and safe, but it’s important to look under the hood. You're heavily exposed to the mega-cap tech names, which is fine for AI, but also to a long tail of traditional SaaS, digital middlemen, legacy enterprise software, and overvalued "digital transformation" companies that are structurally vulnerable to exactly what's happening. You're also implicitly betting on the same economic model that's being disrupted. Software will become cheaper to make, but software will not become worthless. So that doesn't mean sell everything because a tracker like that will always rebalance. But for me it means: be intentional.  Here's how I think about building a portfolio for the next 5 years:  1. Get AI exposure, but be realistic about where the upside actually lives The obvious names are already priced. The companies building the actual intelligence, the ones with the real potential already had their price discovery in private markets. That said, exposure still makes sense. Just be focused about what you're buying. We don’t know what AI companies will take the cake and I’m not that sure that they will be willing to share. Overall an AI-focused ETF gives you broad exposure to the infrastructure layer. Chips, cloud, data centres, the picks and shovels. You're not getting OpenAI's upside, you're getting a basket of companies that grow as AI adoption grows. That's a reasonable bet. It's not asymmetric, but it's not nothing either. What I'd look for: beneficiaries that exist outside this circle of obvious names. There’s loads of sectors that can profit off AI automation heavily. Robotics ETF is also ‘only’ up like 10% in a year.  2. Real assets: own things that can't be copied In a world where digital products get rebuilt overnight, physical scarcity becomes a stronger value proposition, not a weaker one. Real estate is the obvious play for those with capital, but be selective. Residential in supply-constrained markets. Industrial and logistics (AI needs physical warehouses, data centres, grid infrastructure). Not speculative commercial in B-grade locations. For those without the capital or appetite for direct property REITs offer exposure to specific asset types without the illiquidity. Look for REITs focused on infrastructure, logistics, or residential. Not office-heavy (I think triple A locations are of great importance here and if you buy a general office REIT you could be doing the same as buying a Vanguard World as mentioned earlier). Not retail-heavy. The principle: own what can't be replicated by a model running on a server. Oh and yes, AI powered robots could eventually make real estate less scarce, hence why I keep mentioning triple A locations. They will keep their scarcity.  3. The ETF layer: build a "Physical Bunker" This is where I spent the most time. I ran constant feedback loops; LLMs, Perplexity and scenario modelling to build a shortlist that covers the major trends without pretending to predict which one wins. The mental model I used: antifragility. Not just protection from downside, but a portfolio that captures upside from AI productivity while sitting on a hard floor of physical assets that software cannot disrupt. The four I landed on: L&G Clean Water (XMLC). Water is non-discretionary. Predicted 40% supply-demand gap by 2030. And something some people miss: AI data centres consume enormous amounts of water for cooling. Even if this doesn’t directly benefit the ETF companies the narrative cannot be unseen. iShares Global Infrastructure (IQQI). AI development is physically limited by energy and grid capacity. These companies own the infrastructure the intelligence explosion runs on. Steady, regulated returns, with structural tailwinds from something most infrastructure ETFs weren't originally designed to capture. Xtrackers MSCI World Consumer Staples (XDWS). People eat and maintain hygiene regardless of AI's impact on employment. High pricing power in inflationary environments. This is the sleep-well holding. Best protection in stagflation or mass unemployment scenarios. Xtrackers MSCI World Health Care (XDWH). Healthcare is a primary AI beneficiary and structurally defensive. Demographics drive constant demand. GLP-1 and AI-assisted diagnostics drive growth. It's one of the rare sectors that benefits from disruption rather than suffering from it.  I also looked at agriculture ETFs seriously. The food shortage thesis is real. But pricing pressure keeps the upside capped, too much structural complexity. Left it out. Obviously with the geopolitical situation a Defense ETF makes sense too, I didn’t include it for now because I also took into account timing/recent results. Precious metals (gold, silver) deserve a mention here too, the same logic applies. Physical, scarce, and no software can rebuild them. They’ve seen major rallies already. This ETF portfolio is designed to perform in 3.5 out of 5 major economic scenarios: AI bubble, AI boom, mass unemployment, stagflation, and AGI. In my opinion you cannot hedge for AGI which means we can only plan for 4 scenarios. 3.5 out of 4 is a good score.  4. One more thing: Crypto and AI Agents Short version, it’s the most speculative part. Crypto sentiment right now is somewhere between exhausted and absolute despair. However looking at recent OpenClaw developments (The platform for autonomous AI agents running your business) its showing us a world where AI agents could rely heavily on crypto. Using the traditional banking system is difficult, crypto payments make it much easier. I think it will make sense to have a bit of exposure (apart from the Bitcoin-case in general); There is never better timing than during a period of terrible sentiment.  The thread running through all of this: value is shifting. It went from physical to digital, and now back away from things that exist only as logic on a screen. Toward physical scarcity, biological necessity, and the infrastructure that the intelligence revolution actually runs on. The SaaS repricing was only the opening act. Position accordingly.  A portfolio is very personal and clearly there is no *one size fits all* solution, hope this post gives you at least one insight you didn't have yet.  Not financial advice, just my thoughts. None of this is sponsored. Do your own research. Do your own research. Do your own research.

War, Gold, and Crypto Where Does Capital Move During Geopolitical Shocks?  War is not only a military event. It reshapes capital flows, monetary policy, and investor psychology. Whenever geopolitical tension rises, three assets immediately enter the conversation:  Gold Silver Bitcoin  The First Reaction: Flight to Safety  When war begins, markets move into risk-off mode.  Investors typically sell equities, reduce exposure to volatile assets, increase cash holdings, and rotate capital into gold as a defensive allocation.  Gold has functioned as a store of value for thousands of years. During:  Wars Currency collapses Banking crises High inflation periods  gold is perceived as:  Independent of government default risk Physically scarce Universally recognized Historically stable  In moments of panic, capital seeks perceived stability. Gold benefits immediately from this reflex.  Why Crypto Often Falls First?  Bitcoin occupies a unique and sometimes contradictory position in global markets.  It is perceived as both:  A high-volatility technology asset A potential “digital gold”  During the initial shock phase of war, markets usually treat Bitcoin as a risk asset.  This means:  Leveraged positions are liquidated Liquidity tightens Investors reduce exposure to volatility  As a result, Bitcoin often drops alongside equities in the first wave of geopolitical panic.  What Changes as the Conflict Continues?  As war extends, second-order effects begin to appear:  Capital controls Banking restrictions Currency devaluation Payment system disruptions  At this stage, crypto can transform from “risk asset” into financial infrastructure alternative.  Bitcoin becomes relevant because it is:  Borderless Censorship resistant Permissionless  Not dependent on banking rails  In regions facing sanctions or financial restrictions, crypto demand can rise significantly.  The narrative shifts from speculation to utility.  Silver’s More Complex Role Silver behaves differently from gold.  Unlike gold, silver is both:  A store of value An industrial metal  If war slows global economic activity:  Industrial demand for silver may fall Silver may underperform gold If monetary expansion accelerates: Silver can rise alongside gold  Silver reflects both economic growth expectations and monetary conditions, making its behavior more nuanced.  Wars are expensive.  Governments typically respond with:  Increased borrowing, Expanded fiscal spending, Monetary expansion  This increases long-term inflation expectations.  When inflation fears rise, capital often rotates into:  Gold Scarce commodities Bitcoin (due to its fixed 21 million supply)  This is where Bitcoin’s “digital gold” narrative gains strength.  The longer the monetary expansion cycle persists, the stronger this thesis becomes.  Historically, geopolitical shocks follow a pattern:  Stage 1 – Shock  Sell risk Buy gold Hold cash  Stage 2 – Uncertainty  Dollar strength Liquidity preference  Stage 3 – Inflation Concerns  Hard assets rise Gold strengthens Bitcoin may join the move  Bitcoin often becomes attractive not at the moment of panic, but during the monetary consequences of war.  1973 Oil Crisis and Inflation Shock  Following the Yom Kippur War and the subsequent oil embargo, energy prices surged and inflation accelerated across developed economies. Gold, which had only recently detached from the Bretton Woods system, began a multi‑year rally as investors sought protection against currency debasement and stagflation. The episode reinforced gold’s identity as a hedge against geopolitical and monetary instability.  2008 Global Financial Crisis  Although not a war, the 2008 crisis illustrates how systemic stress reshapes capital flows. In the initial liquidity panic, nearly all assets were sold, including gold. However, once central banks launched aggressive monetary expansion programs, gold entered a strong upward cycle. The pattern mirrored the three‑stage model: liquidation first, monetary consequence later.  March 2020 Pandemic Shock  At the onset of the COVID‑19 crisis, Bitcoin fell sharply alongside equities as global markets rushed into cash. Gold also briefly dipped during the liquidity scramble. Yet as stimulus measures expanded and real yields declined, both gold and Bitcoin entered powerful rallies. This was one of the first periods where Bitcoin began to trade more visibly as a macro asset influenced by monetary conditions.  2022 Russia–Ukraine War  When the conflict escalated in early 2022, gold spiked as investors priced in geopolitical risk. Bitcoin initially declined with broader risk markets. However, in regions affected by sanctions and banking restrictions, crypto usage increased as an alternative settlement and transfer mechanism. The divergence between global macro positioning and local utility became more visible.  These examples reinforce a consistent structure: the first reaction is liquidity and fear, while the second reaction is monetary adaptation. Gold tends to respond immediately to geopolitical stress. Bitcoin’s behavior depends more heavily on whether the market is focused on short‑term risk reduction or long‑term monetary consequences.  Physical vs Digital Safe Haven  Gold is a physical asset with a relatively constrained supply that expands slowly through mining. It has lower volatility compared to Bitcoin and is historically perceived as stable during crises. However, it is difficult to transport across borders in large quantities and remains partially dependent on physical custody and financial intermediaries.  Bitcoin, by contrast, is purely digital and has an absolute supply cap of 21 million coins. It is significantly more volatile than gold, but it can be transferred globally within minutes, stored without physical infrastructure, and offers a higher degree of censorship resistance. Its portability and programmability make it structurally different from traditional safe havens.  Gold is historically trusted and stable. Bitcoin is mobile, programmable, and global, but still volatile.  The difference in volatility is critical. It explains why gold is trusted first, while Bitcoin’s role evolves over time.  War does not affect crypto in a single direction.  Short term: Bitcoin behaves like a risk asset.  Medium term: Banking stress increases crypto relevance.  Long term: Monetary expansion strengthens scarce asset narratives.  Gold remains the established safe haven. Bitcoin is still in the process of defining its identity.  The real question is:  In moments of crisis, how does the market categorize Bitcoin?  As speculative technology?  Or as emerging digital hard money?  The answer determines how crypto behaves when the world becomes unstable.

JAPAN and the GLOBAL MARGIN CALL?   For those that need to organize and understand at a 12th grade language! :)  Japan as the Linchpin Yen Carry Trade: Japan has been offering very low interest rates for a long time. Investors borrow money in Japan (Yen) at these low rates and invest it in other countries where they can get higher returns. This is known as the Yen carry trade.  Inflation and Interest Rates: Recently, Japan has been facing inflation, which means the prices of goods and services are going up. To combat inflation, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) might decide to raise interest rates.  Impact on Carry Trade: If the BOJ raises interest rates, it becomes more expensive for investors to borrow money in Japan. This could lead to a situation where investors start selling their investments in other countries to pay back their loans in Japan.  How This Collapses the Market Short Squeeze: When investors start selling their investments to pay back their loans, it can cause a short squeeze. This means that the value of the Yen starts to rise quickly because there's a sudden demand for it.  Global Margin Call: The sudden selling of investments can lead to a global margin call. This is like a chain reaction where one investor selling causes others to sell, leading to a widespread sell-off in the markets.  Flight to Safety: In times of market uncertainty, investors often move their money into safer assets like U.S. Treasuries, gold, and the U.S. dollar. This can cause these assets to rise in value while riskier assets like stocks fall.  Economic Impact: The sell-off in the markets can have a ripple effect on the global economy. Companies may struggle to raise capital, consumer confidence may drop, and economic growth could slow down.  SO NET NET:  Japan is the linchpin because its actions can set off a chain reaction in the global financial markets.   If the BOJ raises interest rates to combat inflation, it could lead to a short squeeze in the Yen, causing investors to sell their investments in other countries.   This sell-off could trigger a global margin call, leading to a collapse in the markets as investors rush to safer assets. The economic impact of such a collapse could be significant, affecting companies, consumers, and overall economic growth.

Geopolitics is back at the center of crypto sentiment.  Developments in the Middle East, especially around Iran and the US, continue to shape market psychology, creating a constant push and pull between risk-on optimism and flight-to-safety behavior.  Crypto is no longer trading in isolation.  When tensions rise, traders do not look only at charts, on-chain flows, or ETF data. They also watch oil, the dollar, Treasury yields, gold, and headlines around military or diplomatic escalation.  That is why the market reaction has been mixed.  On one side, crypto is still seen as a high-beta risk asset. In periods of uncertainty, investors often reduce exposure, rotate into cash, and cut leverage.  On the other side, Bitcoin in particular is increasingly viewed by some as a hedge against instability, monetary stress, and geopolitical fragmentation.  This creates a two-speed market:  - Altcoins often react like pure risk assets and suffer when macro fear rises, - Bitcoin sometimes sells off first with broader risk markets, then stabilizes faster as investors reassess its role  That divergence matters.  The Iran-US angle adds another layer because it affects not only headlines, but also energy markets, inflation expectations, and global liquidity conditions.  If oil spikes:  - inflation fears can return, - rate-cut expectations may weaken, - macro pressure on risk assets can increase.  That is not just a regional story, it becomes a global pricing story.  For crypto, liquidity is everything.  And geopolitical stress can tighten financial conditions very quickly:  - higher volatility, - stronger dollar demand, - lower speculative appetite, - more defensive positioning across portfolios.  In that environment, crypto sentiment becomes fragile even when long-term conviction remains intact.  But there is a paradox here.  Every geopolitical shock reminds the market why borderless, censorship-resistant, globally transferable assets matter.  So while short-term flows may move toward safety, the broader narrative for decentralized assets can actually strengthen over time.  This is why current sentiment feels conflicted.  Traders are balancing two ideas at once:  - “Geopolitical stress is bad for risk assets,” - “Geopolitical stress reinforces the long-term case for neutral digital assets.”  Both can be true simultaneously.  In the near term, markets will likely remain headline-sensitive.  Any signal of escalation or de-escalation involving Iran and the US can quickly change:  - risk appetite, - volatility levels, - safe-haven demand, - positioning across crypto.  Expect fast reactions, sharp reversals, and narrative-driven moves.  Bottom line:  Middle East tensions are not just background noise for crypto anymore. They are a core macro driver of sentiment.  For now, the market is stuck between fear and conviction, between deleveraging and accumulation, between risk-off pressure and the search for alternative stores of value.  That tension is defining crypto right now.

Everyone is celebrating USDT hitting $150 billion in supply Analysts are calling it a liquidity signal A sign capital is flowing back into crypto  They’re not wrong But while everyone is focused on the number Nobody is asking the question that actually matters Is your stablecoin actually stable  Most people think stablecoin risk died with UST in 2022 The $50B algorithmic collapse The Luna death spiral The total wipeout That was the loud version  The quiet version is what you need to understand  In March 2023, USDC the second largest stablecoin in the world fell to $0.87 No hack No exploit No crash Just news that $3.3 billion of its reserves were sitting in Silicon Valley Bank when it collapsed Panic did the rest within hours  And it didn’t stop at USDC DAI depegged because USDC was more than half its collateral USDP fell to $0.91 GUSD fell to $0.96  One bank failure triggered a chain reaction across multiple stablecoins simultaneously  Meanwhile, USDT briefly traded at $1.15 as people rushed out of the affected coins One coin’s crisis became another coin’s flight-to-safety  This is how the market actually works under stress  And it’s not just bank exposure that causes this  In 2025, sUSD fell to $0.68 Not from a hack Not from a bank failing Just a protocol update that changed collateral requirements at the wrong time  There was also USDR Overcollateralized on paper Backed by real estate tokens Looked safe by every metric  But when mass redemptions hit The real estate couldn’t be sold fast enough to honor withdrawals The peg collapsed anyway  This is the lesson most investors miss “Backed” and “liquid” are not the same word  There were over 600 depeg events involving major stablecoins in 2023 alone Most were small Most recovered quickly Most holders never noticed  But the ones that didn’t recover wiped people out completely  So what does an investor actually watch for  What backs the coin fiat, crypto, algorithm, or real assets Where are the reserves held and who holds them Can you redeem directly or only trade on secondary markets How liquid is the collateral when stress hits What happens to coins that use this one as collateral  Stablecoins were designed to be the safe part of your portfolio The place you park when markets get chaotic  But chaos is exactly when their weaknesses surface  $150 billion in USDT is only as stable as the system behind it Not a vault A promise  Everyone wants to buy the dip But nobody checks if their dry powder survives the crash first  As an investor your job is to know the difference before the market Code, research, analysis, customer support, admin work, content, legal drafting, back office labor, and eventually robotics-linked physical work all face deflationary pressure. It does not fix insurance. It does not make healthcare sane. It does not erase tariffs. It does not cheapen electricity when data centers are devouring power. It does not cancel fiscal deficits or Treasury supply. It can make work cheaper while life remains expensive.  That is the real regime split.  Deflation for labor. Inflation for essentials. Productivity for capital. Pressure for households.  That is the world emerging underneath the data. If inflation falls because AI productivity is surging, long-duration tech rips. If inflation falls because households crack, the first move is earnings stress, credit stress, and defensive rotation. The rally comes later, after policy bends.  Deep down, Cathie is early on the explanation and too clean on the outcome.  The bond market is not declaring that AI has defeated inflation.  It is warning that the economy may be too fragile for the oil shock to survive as inflation.  The signal is darker than her framing.

The altseason calls are running hot right now, but the actual market structure is telling a different story, and the distinction between an altcoin bull run and a full altseason matters because it changes how you position.  Altseason is structural, meaning it happens when capital actively flows out of Bitcoin into the broader market in a way you can verify on the charts. An altcoin bull run is selective, meaning individual coins run on their own catalysts while the aggregate picture stays defensive. Right now the aggregate is in defensive rotation, and three ratios make this clean.  TOTAL2 divided by BTC strips out Bitcoin and shows whether the rest of the crypto market is gaining or losing ground against BTC. For structural altseason to begin, this ratio needs a decisive break above cycle-low support that holds on a weekly close, and that confirmation has not arrived. The ratio is sitting near cycle lows rather than breaking out.  ETHBTC is the classic altseason leading indicator because Ethereum gets the institutional rotation first and then the flow cascades into mid and small caps. Right now ETHBTC is stuck grinding in the same range it has been in for months, which means no cascade has started.  CMC20 versus CMC100 is the third leg, because real altseason sends capital into the tail of the market and smaller coins outperform the mega-caps. Right now CMC20 is outperforming CMC100, which is the textbook defensive rotation pattern rather than the altseason one.  Individual coins hitting all-time highs during this period doesn't change the structural read. You can have HYPE at ATH or a specific AI coin running 10x and the aggregate still hasn't confirmed the bottom or kicked off a full rotation. Those are narratives running on specific catalysts, not market-structure signals.  What would actually flip my view is all three signals confirming at the same time. TOTAL2/BTC would need to reclaim and hold above cycle-low support on a weekly close, ETHBTC would need to break decisively above the range it has been grinding in, and CMC100 would need to start outperforming CMC20 so capital is flowing into the speculative tail rather than concentrating in the mega-caps. Until all three flip together, individual coin ATHs are noise rather than signal.  The reason this matters comes down to how you size positions. If you believe we are in altseason you can buy broadly, because the structural tailwind lifts everything and timing matters less. If you believe we are in an altcoin bull run, you are selective. You pick the coins with the strongest specific catalysts, you don't chase moves already up 80 percent, and you wait for your identified positions to develop their own setups rather than assuming the tide is going to lift them.  That second camp is where I am. There is no broad tide yet, just a rising water level for specific narratives, and knowing which one you are playing is the trade.

India 15% earnings growth comes from banks lending more, consumer staples selling more sachets, and IT companies billing more hours. All of those are volume and GDP-linked. "She wasn't posing for history. She was just trying to get her children to the other side. It was September 1965, in the coastal lowlands of South Vietnam. A mother — her name never recorded by the world — waded into a river with her four children clinging to her body. The U.S. Air Force had ordered everyone out of their village near Qui Nhon. Vietcong fighters had been using the surrounding area to fire on American Marines, and now the bombs were coming. She had no time to pack, no time to plan. She had only her children and the water in front of her. A young Japanese photojournalist named Kyoichi Sawada was there that day. Sawada had begged his editors at United Press International for months to send him to Vietnam. They kept saying no — it was an American conflict, not his to cover. So in early 1965, he used his own vacation time and flew there himself, camera in hand, on his own money. His photographs were so powerful that UPI finally relented and gave him the assignment. That single image — a mother, chest-deep in water, four small children wrapped around her — stopped the world. It was titled Flight to Safety. It went on to win the 1965 World Press Photo of the Year. It earned Sawada the Pulitzer Prize for Photography. It swept the Overseas Press Club Award and the US Camera Achievement Award — all in the same year. Critics called him the finest, most daring photographer working in Indochina. But here is the part that history almost forgot. After the awards ceremonies, after the applause, after the recognition that would have satisfied most — Sawada went looking for her. He searched through villages disrupted by war, through communities scattered by conflict, until he found not just the mother and her children, but the second family that had also been captured in the frame. He found both families. And he gave them every cent of the prize money. Not a portion. All of it. He also made sure each family received a copy of the photograph — so that the woman who had waded through that river with terror in her chest could hold, in her own hands, the image that had moved the entire world. He never spoke publicly about it as an act of generosity. To Sawada, it simply wasn't his story to keep. He understood something that many forget: behind every iconic image is a real human being who never asked to become a symbol. The mother in that river wasn't representing a cause. She was saving her children. The least the world could do — the least he could do — was make sure she knew her struggle had been witnessed with dignity, not just documented for acclaim. Sawada kept working. He kept going back to the front lines — to Vietnam, to the Battle of Hue, to the places other photographers hesitated to enter. Those who knew him described a quiet contradiction: a man so daring that he once ran through a minefield for a photograph, yet so careful that he never removed his helmet in the field. In October 1970, while traveling toward Kirrirom Pass in Cambodia, his car was ambushed. He was 34 years old. He left behind no famous last words. Only photographs — and a legacy of quiet integrity that stands apart from almost anyone else in the history of war photography. Most people who pick up a camera want to capture the world. Kyoichi Sawada captured it — and then tried, in whatever small way he could, to give something back to the people inside the frame. The mother crossed the river to save her children. Sawada crossed something harder — the distance between observer and human being. Not everyone with a camera remembers that behind every photograph, there is still a life being lived. He never forgot."

Momentum vs Low Volatility Just Flashed A 5 Sigma Warning  This chart is showing the spread between U.S. momentum stocks and minimum volatility stocks.  Momentum is the part of the market chasing recent winners. Minimum volatility is the defensive side of the market. Stable businesses. Lower beta. Less excitement. When investors are cautious, capital usually rotates toward low vol names. When they are confident, greedy, or desperate to keep up, they crowd into momentum.  Right now, that spread has pushed to roughly a 5 standard deviation overshoot.  That is an extreme positioning event.  Why 5 Sigma Matters  A 5 sigma move is not just a strong trend. It is a statistical extreme. In a clean normal distribution, it is supposed to be almost impossibly rare. Markets are not clean normal distributions, because markets have leverage, passive flows, options feedback loops, forced rebalancing, quant positioning, career risk, and crowd psychology.  So these events happen more often than textbook math says they should.  But that does not make them harmless.  It means the market has moved far outside normal behavior. At that point, the real question is no longer whether the spread mean reverts. Historically, when factor relationships get this stretched, the probability of eventual violent mean reversion is effectively 100%. The uncertainty is timing, trigger, and path.  That distinction matters.  It does not mean the market must crash tomorrow. It means the trade has become structurally fragile. The more crowded one side becomes, the less room there is for disappointment.  The Historical Pattern  The chart highlights March 2000, June 2008, and February 2021.  Those dates matter because they were moments when investors became too concentrated around one dominant story.  In March 2000, technology was real, but the price paid for the story became detached from reality.  In June 2008, parts of the market still looked resilient even though the economic foundation was already cracking underneath.  In February 2021, zero rates, stimulus, retail speculation, venture optimism, and growth stock euphoria all merged into one trade. Winners were treated like permanent winners.  That is the common thread.  These extremes usually do not appear when everyone is terrified. They appear when investors have become too comfortable with one narrative.  What The Chart Is Really Showing  The market is not simply rising.  It is narrowing.  Capital is crowding into the names and factors that have already worked while defensive stocks are being ignored. That can continue longer than skeptics expect, but once positioning gets this stretched, the risk changes.  The danger is no longer just valuation.  The danger is everyone owning the same trade for the same reason.  The unwind can happen several ways.  •    Momentum stocks fall hard •    Low volatility stocks catch up •    Both happen at the same time •    The headline index stays calm while leadership breaks underneath  That last one is important. A market can look fine at the index level while the internal rotation is already doing real damage.  My Take  This is less about calling for an immediate crash and more about spotting factor rotation risk. Momentum has become too dominant, with AI leaders, high beta growth, and crowded winners priced like today’s leadership is permanent. That is usually where markets become vulnerable.  The trigger does not need to be dramatic. High rates, oil pressure, a firmer dollar, weaker earnings guidance, tighter credit, or one major leadership stock disappointing could be enough. When positioning is this stretched, the spark matters less than the crowding already in the system.  A 5 sigma momentum spread does not mean everything collapses tomorrow. It means confidence has turned into crowding, and once factor crowding reaches this level, history says mean reversion is not optional.  Only the timing is.

6 PLAYBOOKS FOR 6 DIFFERENT MARKET REGIMES  Last week’s firm-wide @smbcapital meeting was about better adapting to different market regimes.  Which begs the question - what types of market regimes are there for discretionary traders? And what playbooks should we be running for each of them?  I’ll start and you all can expand on this in the replies.  Obviously this is far from exhaustive and kept high-level, but I think this should lead serious traders to do some deep reflection of their own.   1. Theme-driven bullish market. Markets like this one favor momentum strategies, swing longs, overnight momentum, IPOs, and headlines relevant to the driving theme.  Early summer of 2026 certainly fell under this with AI as the driver and leading sectors like DRAM / cloud computing.  2. Macro-driven markets. Think in the spring during the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict, think  2025 Trump tariffs and the Russia-Ukraine war. Due to the randomness and volatility of these headlines, this market highly favors breaking news trading as well as trading move-to-move, while greatly reducing overnight exposure and swing exposure.   3. Range-bound market. Think of the last couple months, where we've had no prevailing theme and most indices have stayed range-bound while the leaders from the prior cycle corrected. In this market, you want to reduce overall trading activity and risk allocation. If volatility is inflated, you might focus on selling vol, but you need to be careful of complacency. There can still be niche opportunities, but overall, most traders will find it best to be more hands-off.  4. Panic-driven markets. During these markets, breakdowns can work exceptionally well. However, I found that my greatest PNL, ironically, comes from longs in names that have totally capitulated, especially trading the right side of the V. Overnights and swing trades can again be quite favorable in this market. IPOs and headlines tend to take a back seat.  5. Idiosyncratic single-stock or single-sector moves. This is the type of market where broader themes are quiet, yet single stock names occupy the majority of your focus. This is where all risk should be allocated to the single stock or sector. I'm thinking of when we saw the epic short squeeze in $CAR this year, or prior moves in names like $MSTR, $GME, $AMC, or when sectors offer great opportunities, like the quantum names over the last few years.  6. Euphoria. We've seen markets like this in 2021 following COVID, as well as glimpses of this at times during the last couple years. In this market, small caps are on fire. Anything with a theme works, and momentum breakouts go so much further than you could have imagined. This is when swing trading and big-picture imagination work better than you could have ever imagined. Those that are quick to short or skeptical either miss out or risk ruin, as using your brain can get you killed here.   Further questions from here: 1. How do you identify each of these regimes FOR YOU? For example, one criteria might be a certain vix level or sentiment metric. 2. What playbooks are you competent in for each of those? 3. How much risk do each of these markets deserve?  This post was inspired by thoughts from @steenbab and this blog post: https://t.co/77ifbTYlRJ

Here’s the weekend routine I run to get a full picture of what the market is doing.  1. Review the three major indexes. S&P 500, the Qs, and the Russell 2000. That’s 2,000+ stocks and it goes quick, maybe 20 to 25 minutes. Gives me a feel for the broader market and whether any themes are showing up.  2. Thematic review. Which themes are leading and which are lagging. This is where the rotation shows itself. If money is moving from one space into another I want to see it, because that tells me whether growth is working, tech is working, or it’s consumer staples doing the heavy lifting.  3. My three key watchlists. These are my three edges in the market.  IPOs from the last year. How are the younger stocks being treated, supported or trashed? That tells you where the risk appetite is.  High tight flags. Are there setups that have run 100% in under eight weeks? If there are a lot of them, there’s momentum and juice in the market.  High volume edge. This is the bread and butter. Highest volume in a year, highest volume ever, highest volume since IPO, highest volume since last earnings, all as one scan. That shows me which stocks are exhibiting the edge on price and volume, and those go on the focus list.  All of it paints three things:  1.Risk-on or risk-off 2.If the market is trending, which groups and themes are trending 3.Whether I have enough across the three watchlists to build a focus list for Monday  The most important part is that all of this happens when the market is closed. Same with my daily routine. By the time the market opens I’m looking at two, three, maybe four stocks max, watching levels I already planned. I’m not screening intraday to find ideas.  Most of my work is done while the markets are closed. Most of my execution happens when they’re open.

The market beneath the market  One of the biggest misconceptions in investing is how the stock market actually works. Most people become obsessed with volatility because that’s the only thing they can see. They celebrate when a stock jumps 8% and panic when it falls 8%, as if billions of dollars suddenly appeared or disappeared overnight. In reality, that’s usually not what’s happening.  The US stock market is worth approx $75 trillion, making it one of the largest pools of capital ever assembled. While new money enters the market every day through retirement accounts, pensions, and other investors, most of the day to day movement isn’t driven by fresh money. It’s driven by existing capital constantly being reallocated from one opportunity to another.  A few years ago, investors were selling consumer staples to buy software. Then they sold software to buy AI. Someday they’ll sell AI to buy whatever the next great opportunity becomes. The money didn’t disappear, it simply changed its proverbial addresses.  That’s why I’ve always believed the stock market isn’t just a collection of businesses. It’s also the largest capital allocation machine ever created. Every second of every trading day, trillions of dollars are competing to find what investors believe offers the highest future return.  Most investors think businesses compete only with other businesses, but that’s only half the story. Every business is also competing for capital. A dollar invested in $AMZN is a dollar that can’t be invested in $META, $TSLA, Treasury bills, gold, real estate, or thousands of other opportunities. Every investment has an invisible competitor.  Capital has no emotions and no loyalty. It doesn’t care what worked yesterday or which company investors fell in love with last year. It simply flows toward wherever people believe the best future returns will be found, and the moment those expectations change, the direction of capital changes with them.  This is why your stock can decline even when the business is performing exceptionally well. Maybe a large fund is reducing exposure to technology. Maybe an index is rebalancing. Maybe investors simply found another opportunity they believe offers a better risk adjusted return. The business may not have changed at all. The destination of capital did.  Most investors spend their time watching prices, but prices are simply the footprints capital leaves behind. They tell you where money has already gone, but they rarely explain why it moved there in the first place. If you only watch prices, you’re observing the result instead of understanding the cause.  Once you begin thinking about capital instead of just prices, the market starts to make a lot more sense. You stop asking, “Why did this stock go down today?” and start asking, “Where did the capital go, and why?” Very often, the answer has little to do with the business itself and everything to do with investors repositioning capital.  None of this changes what ultimately matters. In the short run, capital determines where prices go. In the long run, business performance determines where capital goes. That’s why my job isn’t to predict where money will flow next week. It’s to own exceptional businesses that will continue attracting capital over the next decade because they keep creating more value than their competitors.  🌹

There's been a lot of discussion over Terry Smith and the decisions made at Fundsmith. Let me keep it simple for you.  As Warren Buffett warned:  "For the investor, a too-high purchase price for the stock of an excellent company can undo the effects of a subsequent decade of favorable business developments."  Fundsmith's biggest problem was not its "strategy."  Rather, it was severely overpaying for many great businesses and/or holding them through extremely rich valuations that the growth rate simply didn't justify. Remember, a 50x multiple on a business growing earnings at a 25% CAGR is much cheaper than a 30x multiple on a business growing earnings at an 8% CAGR.  Terry Smith has at times attributed the low FCF yields of his holdings to the exceptional quality of the businesses  owned. While there may have been some truth to this, it also implicitly acknowledges that a significant portion of Fundsmith's returns in recent years came from multiple expansion rather than earnings growth.   I had this conversation with several friends years ago during a walk in SF. As history has repeatedly shown, multiples do not expand indefinitely. At some point, they tend to contract — often at the expense of future returns.  That's it. It's that simple.  Is $ROL a great business? Yes. Is it worth the 1.70% FCF Yield that Fundsmith paid for? No.  Is $MTD a great business? Yes. Is it worth the <3.00% FCF Yield that Fundsmith paid for? No.  Is $PG a great business? Yes. Is it worth the <2.50% FCF Yield that Fundsmith paid for? No.   Is $ZTS a great business? Yes. Is it worth the <1.00% FCF Yield that Fundsmith paid for? No.  Is $MKC a good business? Yes. Is it worth the <3.50% FCF Yield that Fundsmith paid for? Not with a mid-single digit growth rate.  Is $BF.B a good business? Yes. Is it worth the <3.00% FCF Yield that Fundsmith paid for? Not with a mid-single digit growth rate (assumed at the time, EPS essentially flat since).  Is $EW a good business? Yes. Is it worth the <2.00% FCF Yield that Fundsmith paid for? No.  At the same time, he's done exceptionally well on names like $MAR (>4.25% FCF Yield at purchase), $GOOGL (~3.75% FCF Yield at purchase), $META, $V, $PM, etc.  It's difficult to continue generating strong returns when paying tech-like multiples for slow-growing businesses, such as consumer staples or companies growing in the low single digits. Most of Fundsmith's best investments occurred when both the valuation was attractive and the underlying growth rate was strong enough for the two to work in tandem (the "twin-engines").  Of course, there will always be exceptions. Some investments where he may have overpaid and still did well, and others where he bought at a reasonable price but didn't do as well. That's  investing — it happens. However, when there's a consistent and large disconnect between the price overpaid and the underlying value and growth of the businesses, it becomes much harder to generate strong long-term returns.  One final point: while it's fair to critique Fundsmith's approach, it's also worth viewing the situation with some perspective and grace. Terry Smith built an excellent track record over many years, and nobody is perfect — we ALL make mistakes in investing. Sure, there's some irony in the fact that many of the high-quality companies he owned saw their multiples expand significantly during a period when they benefited from momentum. Still, the broader lesson remains valuable. As the saying goes, "Only a fool learns from his own mistakes. The wise man learns from the mistakes of others." While many of us have inevitably paid our own tuition to "Wall St University" through our mistakes, there’s a real opportunity to accelerate our growth and learn as investors by thoughtfully studying both the successes and the missteps of well-known figures like Smith.
