WE GIVE UP... SINCE THE INDIANA FEVER DOESN'T SEEM TO CARE ABOUT FIXING THEIR OWN PROBLEMS, WE DID IT FOR THEM.  The Indiana Fever do not have a talent problem.  They do not have a scoring problem.  They do not even have a chemistry problem.  They have an offensive governance problem.  The wrong player is too often allowed to control the possession. The right player is too often removed from the action. One of the league’s most explosive scorers is being permitted to stand, wait and hunt her own shot instead of being coached into becoming the most dangerous off-ball weapon in basketball.  The result is not elite offense.  It is high-level talent playing sophisticated streetball.  And after months of watching the same problems repeat themselves, the numbers now make the diagnosis impossible to ignore:  The Indiana Fever are at their best when Caitlin Clark controls the offense and Kelsey Mitchell participates in it... not when Mitchell tries to become the offense herself.  That is the problem.  That is also the solution.  Caitlin Clark Is Not Merely a Scorer. She Is the System.   The most important number in this entire discussion is not points, field-goal percentage or three-point percentage.  It is this:  Indiana’s net rating with Caitlin Clark on the floor: +1.9 per 100 possessions Indiana’s net rating with Clark off the floor: -10.3  That is a 12.2-point swing.  When Clark plays, the Fever function like a winning team.  When she sits, they function like one of the worst teams in basketball.  That is not the statistical profile of a player who should spend long stretches stationed away from the ball, waiting for the offense to find her.  That is the profile of the player who should be directing every meaningful possession.  Clark is not simply another high-volume guard. She is Indiana’s organizer, pressure release, transition engine and primary source of advantage creation.  Her production reflects it.  Per 36 minutes:  25.5 points 9.5 assists 4.8 rebounds  Kelsey Mitchell, by comparison:  25.8 points 3.1 assists 1.7 rebounds  Their scoring is nearly identical.  Their influence on the game is not.  Clark creates points for herself and everyone around her. Mitchell is overwhelmingly dependent upon scoring to create value.  That distinction should determine the structure of the offense.  Instead, Indiana too often treats the two as interchangeable ball-dominant guards.  They are not.  The Fever Are Confusing Shot-Making With Offensive Execution  Indiana leads the league in scoring at 94.4 points per game.  It ranks first in three-point percentage at 37.7% and third in overall field-goal percentage.  On the surface, that appears to be proof of a highly functioning offense.  It is not.  The Fever rank only sixth in assists.  That tells a very different story.  Indiana is scoring because it has exceptional shot-makers... not because it is consistently producing elite possessions.  There is a major difference.  A disciplined offense creates repeatable advantages through spacing, screening, cutting, timing and ball movement.  A talented but poorly governed offense survives because gifted players repeatedly make difficult shots.  Indiana has been living too heavily in the second category.  That is why the offense can look brilliant for one quarter and completely disjointed the next.  It is why a player can score 30 points while contributing almost nothing else.  It is why Clark can dominate one night and then spend critical possessions removed from the center of the action.  The Fever do not lack offensive talent.  They lack an offensive hierarchy.  Kelsey Mitchell Is Being Allowed to Play a Smaller Version of Her Own Game  Kelsey Mitchell is one of the most explosive scorers in the WNBA.  She is shooting:  49.5% from the field 42.3% from three 54.3% on two-point attempts 62.4% at the rim 61.8% from three to ten feet 62.7% true shooting  Those are elite numbers.  But they also reveal what Indiana is failing to maximize.  Mitchell is devastating when she gets downhill, catches the ball in motion and attacks a rotating defense.  More than 55% of her two-point field goals are assisted.  It means her most efficient interior scoring is frequently being created through someone else’s pass.  In practical terms: cuts, relocations, transition opportunities, secondary actions and catches against an already compromised defense.  That is precisely the version of Mitchell Indiana should be building around.  Instead, too many possessions end with her standing outside the three-point line, waiting for the ball so she can attempt to beat a set defender one-on-one.  She is capable of doing it.  That does not make it good offense.  A difficult shot converted by a great scorer is still often a poorly constructed possession.  The Game-by-Game Results Are Even More Revealing  When Mitchell has made at least five two-point field goals in games alongside Clark, Indiana is:  10–4  Clark and Mitchell combine for 47.1 points per game in those contests.  When Mitchell has made fewer than five two-point baskets, Indiana is:  2–6  Their combined scoring falls to 37.5 points per game.  That is not a minor difference.  It is a 46-point swing in winning percentage.  When Mitchell is cutting, attacking, receiving the ball in motion and scoring inside the arc, Indiana wins at a high rate.  When she becomes primarily a perimeter-based shot creator, Indiana’s efficiency and winning percentage collapse.  The numbers do not say Mitchell should stop scoring.  They say Indiana must change how she scores.  When Clark and Mitchell Both Play Heavy Minutes, Playmaking Makes a Difference.  In games where Clark and Mitchell both played at least 30 minutes, the Fever went 6–5.  When Mitchell recorded at least two assists in those games, Indiana went:  6–3  When she recorded one assist or fewer:  0–2  When Mitchell reached at least three assists, Indiana went 4–2.  The sample is not enormous, but the basketball logic is unmistakable.  When Mitchell participates in the offense rather than merely finishing possessions, Indiana becomes more difficult to guard.  The defense can no longer load toward her shot.  Clark can attack a moving floor.  Boston can operate against late help.  Cutters receive the ball before the defense resets.  The offense becomes connected.  That is the difference between five talented players occupying the court and five players functioning as a unit.  Mitchell’s On-Off Numbers Should Alarm the Organization  Indiana’s net rating with Mitchell on the floor is +7.8.  With her off the floor, it is +10.7.  The Fever have been 2.9 points better per 100 possessions with Mitchell off the court.  That does not mean Mitchell is a bad player.  It means her scoring production is not translating into the level of team dependence expected from a player with her usage, minutes and offensive freedom.  Her usage rate is 27.2%.  She plays 32.5 minutes per game.  She averages:  23.3 points 2.8 assists 1.6 rebounds 1.0 steal 0.1 blocks  She is producing elite scoring with remarkably little peripheral impact.  That is not an argument to reduce her role.  It is an argument to redefine it.  The Coaching Failure Is Structural  This is where responsibility shifts from the player to the coaching staff.  Players generally repeat what a system permits.  If Mitchell is allowed to stand outside the arc, wait for the ball, reject movement and repeatedly attack one-on-one, then that is not merely a player habit.  It is the offense.  If Clark is permitted to spend possessions away from the ball while a less complete creator controls the action, then that is not an accident.  It is a coaching decision.  If Indiana’s best cutter can abandon cutting for an entire half without immediate correction, then the staff is not enforcing offensive standards.  That is why this issue extends beyond Mitchell.  The broader problem is that Stephanie White and her staff have not established a disciplined offensive identity.  The Fever frequently appear to have concepts without rules, talent without hierarchy and freedom without accountability.  Elite basketball does not operate that way.  The best teams define:  who initiates; where the first advantage comes from; what each player does when the ball is elsewhere; how spacing is preserved; when isolation is appropriate; and what happens when the first action fails.  Indiana too often appears to define none of it firmly enough.  The players are left to improvise.  And improvisation without structure is streetball, regardless of how talented the participants may be.  The Fix  The solution is not complicated.  Caitlin Clark must orchestrate the offense  Clark should initiate the overwhelming majority of half-court possessions when she is on the floor.  Not because Mitchell cannot dribble.  Because Clark sees more, creates more and elevates more.  Her job is not merely to score.  Her job is to organize the entire defense and decide where the advantage will appear.  Kelsey Mitchell must become an elite off-ball weapon  Mitchell should be cutting, relocating, sprinting off screens and attacking closeouts.  Her speed should force defenders to make decisions before she catches the ball.  She should receive more passes while moving toward the basket and fewer while standing 24 feet away from it.  The goal is not fewer Mitchell points.  The goal is easier Mitchell points.  Aliyah Boston must become part of the connective tissue  Boston should screen, short roll, facilitate and punish switches.  Clark-Boston actions should force the first defensive rotation.  Mitchell’s movement should punish the second.  That creates a layered offense instead of a sequence of isolated attacks.  The staff must enforce possession standards  Standing still cannot be optional.  Ball-watching cannot be tolerated.  Repeated one-on-one possessions cannot be mistaken for freedom.  Every player should know what she is expected to do when the ball is not in her hands.  That includes Mitchell.  Especially Mitchell.  The Final Diagnosis  The Indiana Fever have enough talent to become the most dangerous offensive team in the WNBA.  But talent is not the same as organization.  Right now, Indiana is winning too often because its players are capable of overcoming the offense instead of being elevated by it.  The numbers reveal the path forward.  When Clark controls the game, Indiana functions.  When Mitchell moves, cuts and scores within the structure, Indiana wins.  When the Fever abandon those principles, they become ordinary.  This is not a mystery anymore.  The problem has been identified.  The offense must run through Caitlin Clark.  Kelsey Mitchell must stop waiting for the game to come to her and start attacking it without the ball.  And the coaching staff must finally decide whether it wants to supervise talented streetball or coach championship basketball.  Because Indiana already has the players.  What it lacks is the system.

Torsten Slok at Apollo (whose economic impulses I usually agree with) argues the S&P 493 is spending heavily on AI with nothing to show for it. I strongly disagree.  Slok: "The S&P 493 is spending heavily on AI. But it is not showing up in profit margins, see the first chart below. Looking at the individual sectors of the S&P 500 outside tech shows that the picture is flat, cyclical or worse, see charts 2, 3 and 4. Health care margins have halved since 2015; consumer staples are stuck near 6% and consumer discretionary near 8%; energy and materials have given back most of their 2022-23 gains; real estate is going sideways; and the only genuine improvements look like an ordinary cyclical recovery rather than a technology-driven step change. The bottom line is that the AI capex boom is so far only showing up in the sellers' margins, not the buyers'. This is important because the longer it takes the S&P 493 to generate ROI, the bigger the downside risks to an economy and a market this concentrated in the AI trade." (Link: https://t.co/AyMyJINWyL…)  I strongly disagree with this reasoning.  Margins are one component of returns on capital, not the returns itself (NOPAT margin × invested capital turnover = ROIC). The deeper issue is that the argument implicitly assumes AI productivity gains should accrue to the adopting company as higher margins. They absolutely do not have to... and in a competitive market, they won't.  Buffett described almost exactly this scenario in the 1985 Berkshire letter, on textile machinery:  "Over the years, we had the option of making large capital expenditures in the textile operation that would have allowed us to somewhat reduce variable costs. Each proposal to do so looked like an immediate winner. Measured by standard return-on-investment tests, in fact, these proposals usually promised greater economic benefits than would have resulted from comparable expenditures in our highly-profitable candy and newspaper businesses.But the promised benefits from these textile investments were illusory. Many of our competitors, both domestic and foreign, were stepping up to the same kind of expenditures and, once enough companies did so, their reduced costs became the baseline for reduced prices industrywide. Viewed individually, each company's capital investment decision appeared cost-effective and rational; viewed collectively, the decisions neutralized each other and were irrational (just as happens when each person watching a parade decides he can see a little better if he stands on tiptoes)."  That is my (strong) base case for AI adoption. Each deployment pencils out, everyone deploys, costs fall industry-wide, prices follow costs down, and the economic benefit lands with the customer vs. shareholders. Aggregate ROIC doesn't move because capitalism is designed to compete excess returns away. Returns will only durably improve for the handful of businesses whose moats let them capture and hold the surplus.  So flat 493 margins aren't evidence AI isn't working. They're roughly what you'd expect if it is working and the gains are being passed through as consumer surplus. Berkshire kept funding those mills for years precisely because each project looked rational in isolation. CapEx that has a competitive-necessity doesn't require a margin payoff to begin (or to persist).

Someone sent me a monthly letter from a Singapore-based fund showing Indonesian consumer staples trading at only 8.48x forward P/E, versus a 15-year average of roughly 19x.  At first glance, it looks absurdly cheap.  My view: there are very good reasons why it is cheap, and anyone expecting Indonesian staples to simply mean-revert back to 20x, 25x or 30x P/E is probably looking at the wrong Indonesia.  The good old days when Indonesian consumer staples routinely commanded 25x to 30x earnings are way, way behind us. Valuation ultimately comes down to two things: Earnings × the multiple investors are willing to pay for those earnings.  On the earnings side, many Indonesian staples remain remarkably resilient. The problem is the second part of the equation. The market is no longer willing to pay the same multiple for Indonesian consumption.  Why?  Because the structural consumer story has deteriorated. Job creation in Indonesia sucks. Good job creation sucks even more. We can celebrate a historically low unemployment rate all we want, but if people are increasingly absorbed into informal, low-productivity employment and the overwhelming majority of new workers earn very little, that does not create the next generation of consuming middle class.  Even among people who managed to find jobs over the past decade, roughly 80% were earning below Rp3 million per month, around US$170. Think about what that means for the consumer ladder.  The entire old Indonesia staples thesis was built around millions of households climbing from subsistence consumption into discretionary consumption: better nutrition, branded foods, personal care, healthcare, dairy products, restaurants, travel and financial services.  But if income progression stalls, the ladder stops moving. You still sell shampoo. You still sell instant noodles. You still sell medicine. But investors stop paying 30x earnings for 5% growth.  That is exactly what happened to Unilever Indonesia. UNVR once traded around 50x P/E because investors were willing to pay an enormous premium for the Indonesian middle-class growth story. Today, nobody cares that it used to trade at 50x. The stock has derated toward the mid-teens because the market changed its assessment of the growth opportunity.  That is the important lesson from this chart.  A stock does not become cheap simply because it trades below its historical multiple. Sometimes the historical multiple was pricing a country that no longer exists.  Of course, there are still bright spots. Cimory ($CMRY), for example, continues to deliver attractive earnings growth because the underlying sector thesis remains compelling. Indonesia's dairy consumption is still relatively low, domestic milk production is insufficient to meet demand, and rising protein consumption should structurally benefit the category.  But even CMRY's share price struggles to break away meaningfully.  Why? Because bottom-up excellence can only fight top-down gravity for so long.  There simply are not enough active foreign investors left looking at Indonesia deeply enough to discover and continuously support stories like CMRY.  And that brings us to the second problem, which has almost nothing to do with consumers.  Indonesia's capital market itself became distorted.  From roughly 2023 until early 2026, Indonesia stopped being primarily an earnings market and became a conglomerate stock market.  Capital poured into concentrated, low-float stocks belonging to large business groups.  Remember the period when the Prajogo Pangestu-linked stocks were trading at 300x, 400x, even 500x earnings, and somehow the stocks kept outperforming?  That liquidity had to come from somewhere. Indonesia does not have an infinite pool of institutional capital. Money flowing into one part of the market means money is leaving another part.  Domestic fund managers were essentially given two choices. Play the conglomerate stocks. Or underperform the index.  Those who joined the trade reduced positions elsewhere, including consumer staples.  Those who refused to participate watched their relative performance collapse, suffered redemptions, and were subsequently forced to sell even more of the stocks they actually liked.  This created an extraordinary feedback loop. Conglomerate stocks went up. Their index weights increased. More passive money was forced into them. Traditional stocks lost weight. Fund managers sold traditional stocks to fund the new benchmark exposures. Their prices fell. Their weights fell again. More money left.  Indonesia's conglomerate boom did not merely inflate conglomerate valuations. It cannibalized the rest of the market.  That is why I think the timing in this chart is extremely revealing. The structural collapse in staples multiples accelerated precisely during the period when Indonesia's market became increasingly dominated by conglomerate stocks.  And because Indonesia is a relatively small weight within MSCI Emerging Markets, index inclusion is almost a zero-sum game. One in, one out lol When another giant conglomerate stock enters MSCI, something else needs to lose weight or leave.  Names such as Kalbe Farma ($KLBF), Indofood ($INDF) and Indofood CBP ($ICBP) became casualties of this combination of derating, relative underperformance and changing index composition. I think Charoen Pokphand Indonesia ($CPIN) could be one of the next victims if the relative market-cap and liquidity dynamics continue moving against it.  This is why simply saying, "Staples are trading at 8.5x versus a 19x historical average, therefore buy," is far too simplistic.  Yes, the sector is trading at roughly 55% below its 15-year average multiple. But historical mean reversion requires the forces that created the historical mean to still exist. Today, several of them do not.  So can Indonesian staples rerate now that the conglomerate-stock pumping cycle appears to be ending?  Possibly.  If domestic institutional investors rotate back toward fundamentals, staples are an obvious destination. Balance sheets are generally cleaner, earnings visibility is better, cash flows are real, governance is easier to understand, and valuations have already been destroyed.  But there is another problem: Who is the marginal buyer? Domestic mutual-fund AUM needs to recover. Domestic fund managers need inflows before they can meaningfully rebuild positions.  And I seriously doubt foreign active managers are suddenly going to rush back into Indonesian staples.  Indonesia's weight in MSCI EM is now only around 0.4% lol At 0.4%, a global emerging-market portfolio manager can practically ignore Indonesia and still sleep perfectly well.  That is incredibly important for valuation. A market rerates when incremental capital competes for assets. If there are very few incremental buyers, cheap stocks can remain cheap for years.  And the foreign-investor problem goes beyond country weight. Indonesia's capital-market ecosystem desperately needs new faces.  Many Indonesian sell-side institutions have effectively lost credibility with serious foreign institutional investors. Talk to investors in Singapore or Hong Kong and Indonesia has developed an ugly reputation as a market where foreign investors are sometimes treated less as partners in price discovery and more as exit liquidity for domestic players.  That reputation is toxic.  And find me a really good Indonesian institutional salesperson today who can sit in front of a global fund manager and discuss ROIC, competitive dynamics, channel checks, capital allocation, industry structure and valuation at the level expected in Singapore, Hong Kong, New York or London.  Maybe zero.  You cannot complain that foreigners do not invest in Indonesia while simultaneously destroying the research, governance, liquidity and market structure required to attract them.  So what would actually make me structurally bullish on Indonesian staples again?  Not merely lower interest rates. Not another consumer stimulus package. Not stocks becoming "cheap."  Indonesia needs to rebuild the middle-class formation machine. Create good jobs. Pay people good salaries. Increase productivity. Move workers from informal employment into productive formal employment. Give households confidence that next year's income will be higher than this year's. Then consumption upgrades naturally.  That is what eventually drives sustainable volume growth, premiumization and operating leverage for consumer companies.  And separately, Indonesia must repair its capital market. Restore credible price discovery. Increase genuine free float. Clean up nominee structures. Bring serious foreign institutional investors back. Rebuild the quality of sell-side research and institutional sales. Grow domestic mutual-fund AUM. Stop designing a market where a handful of concentrated stocks can suck liquidity out of hundreds of fundamentally healthier companies.  Only then can the valuation architecture normalize.  Until those things happen, I would be extremely careful using Indonesia's historical consumer-staples multiple as a valuation anchor.  The chart says 8.48x versus a 19x historical mean.  Someone might look at it and see a screaming buy. I look at it and see the market delivering a message.  Indonesia's staples are not only being priced for lower earnings growth. They are being priced for weaker middle-class formation, weaker institutional liquidity, weaker foreign participation and a fundamentally lower willingness to pay for the Indonesia consumer story.  Some individual companies will absolutely outperform. CMRY can grow. ICBP can compound. INDF can generate cash. KLBF can remain resilient. CPIN can deliver excellent cycles. But a good company does not automatically deserve its old multiple.  For the entire sector to sustainably rerate, Indonesia needs something much bigger than better quarterly earnings. It needs to rebuild both the consumer and the market that used to pay a premium for that consumer.  Until then, 8.5x may look cheap compared with history. But history is not obligated to come back.

Why Stocks Exploded Higher Today  The strongest explanation for today’s equity rally is not that a massive wave of new money suddenly entered the financial system.  Several pressures weighing on valuations eased at the same time while investors aggressively returned to large technology and AI related stocks.  Crude fell sharply. Long term Treasury yields declined. Inflation fears eased at the margin. Volatility remained subdued. Bitcoin, copper and other risk assets also strengthened.  Together, that created a powerful risk on environment.  Oil Changed the Immediate Macro Equation  Lower crude reduces the probability of the most extreme inflation outcomes and improves expectations for future business and household costs.  Markets do not need diesel, freight or transportation expenses to normalize immediately. They only need investors to believe the future environment may be less damaging than previously expected.  That appears to be what happened today.  The important caveat is that refining constraints and extremely expensive diesel remain. Lower crude therefore provides relief without proving the broader energy shock has been solved.  Bonds Confirm Relief But Not A Fed Pivot  The Treasury market provides another important clue.  The 10 year yield fell toward 4.96%, reducing some of the discount rate pressure on equities.  But the 2 year remained around 4.74% and barely declined.  That distinction matters enormously.  The market is removing some longer term inflation and term premium pressure without substantially changing expectations for restrictive near term Federal Reserve policy.  The Fed has not pivoted.  The bond market is saying conditions became somewhat less hostile, not that monetary policy suddenly became easy.  Technology Magnified Everything  Large semiconductor and technology companies posted substantial gains.  Because the S&P 500 is weighted by market capitalization, moves in its largest companies have an outsized influence on the index.  That helps explain how equities can surge even while much of the broader economy remains uneven.  And more than $1 trillion being added to stock market capitalization does not mean $1 trillion of cash actually entered stocks.  Marginal transactions can reprice trillions of dollars of existing shares.  The Cross Asset Signal  Today’s combination is remarkably coherent.  Stocks rose.  Bitcoin and other crypto assets rallied.  Copper strengthened.  Treasury yields declined.  Oil fell.  Gold weakened.  The dollar remained firm.  That does not resemble a classic recession panic or geopolitical flight to safety.  It looks much more like investors reducing the amount of near term inflation and financial risk they were pricing while continuing to embrace growth and AI exposure.  What Could Make This Fragile  The biggest question is whether cheaper crude eventually translates into cheaper delivered energy.  If diesel remains extremely expensive, refining capacity stays impaired and transportation costs remain elevated, the inflation constraint has not disappeared.  That would leave the Fed restrictive even while markets celebrate lower crude.  The rally becomes far more convincing if energy costs continue easing, credit remains stable, market participation broadens and yields decline without growth collapsing.  If crude is instead falling because demand is weakening while diesel stays expensive and credit conditions deteriorate, today’s rally will look very different in hindsight.  The market did not suddenly decide the economy is healthy.  It decided the immediate downside looked less severe.  That was enough to produce a powerful rally.  Whether it becomes something more durable will depend on energy, credit, yields and whether the broader economy eventually confirms what equities are already pricing.

Then look at sectors such as real estate, consumer staples and utilities. The damage from higher rates becomes increasingly obvious.  So the idea that 5.3% yields aren't affecting stocks because the S&P 500 remains near record highs misses what is actually happening.  Rates ARE impacting the market. Technology doesn't necessarily need to crash. Instead, money could rotate into value and other neglected areas, allowing broader participation to improve while the overall market continues higher.  *  So, the bottom line: 5.3% yields haven't failed to hurt stocks. Alright guys, a lot of you have been asking for my thoughts on the market and what I expect next for $BTC, $IREN, $NBIS, $CIFR, the rest of the neoclouds and the broader AI trade.  So here they are.  What we are seeing right now looks much more like a violent leverage flush than the beginning of a structural bear market.  Since early September, we had already been tracking one of the biggest warnings, which was the CCC credit spreads were widening.  That told us that the weakest and most leveraged companies were starting to feel the pressure from higher borrowing costs.   CoreWeave became one of the clearest examples, with the market starting to question how aggressively these companies were financing their AI infrastructure buildouts.  That is exactly why we were maintaining a moderate-to-high cash allocation of roughly 25%, while keeping the rest of the portfolio diversified across multiple industries.  I talked about it here:  https://t.co/dosersaSut  Fast-forward a few weeks, and the rest of the market has finally started focusing on the same problem.  Now suddenly everyone is panicking, everyone is talking about debt, and everyone is calling for the AI bubble to burst.  I still don’t think that is what is happening.  There are two major reasons.  First, AI demand remains extremely strong. The AI cycle does not end because financing becomes more expensive for a few weeks. The real warning sign would be hyperscalers cutting their CapEx plans, slowing infrastructure expansion and showing weaker demand for compute.  We are not there yet.  Second, AI has become a strategic priority for the United States.  The competition with China is no longer just about better consumer products. It involves software, compute infrastructure, frontier models, semiconductors and national security.  That gives the AI buildout a strategic component that didn't exist during the dot-com bubble.  That does not mean every AI company survives or every project makes money.   Some companies are overleveraged, some projects will fail and some valuations deserve to compress.  But that is very different from saying the entire AI cycle is finished.  The macro environment is also clearly not helping right now.  Financial conditions are tight, yields remain elevated, credit has started reacting and geopolitical uncertainty continues to push investors toward risk-off positioning.  But moving into the next several days, I think we are getting close to a bottoming formation.  Several of our Cryptic Indicators are now sitting at some of their most overextended levels since April 2025, and in some cases at the most extreme readings we have recorded.  My base case is that we begin seeing a bottom form over roughly the next 5–7 days, followed by stabilization and eventually a broader reversal.  That is why I only started buying aggressively again over the past few days.  I am gradually increasing exposure to my core neocloud positions such as $IREN, $CIFR, $NBIS and $APLD, while also adding selectively across semiconductors including $MU, $AMD, $ASML, $INTC and others.  I believe a lot of people are going to look back at this period as a major opportunity they missed because they allowed fear to take over.  And I do NOT think this is another dot-com bubble.  The market structure is very different. Many of the companies driving the AI cycle today are producing enormous revenues and cash flows, hyperscalers are still committing massive amounts of capital, and AI infrastructure has both a commercial and strategic use case.  The highly leveraged neoclouds clearly carry more financing risk, which is exactly why we were tracking credit in the first place.  But again, expensive financing does not automatically mean bad economics if the returns generated on that capital remain higher than the cost of funding.  This is why I continue to view what is happening as a:  MID-CYCLE CORRECTION.  Not a bear market.  And definitely NOT the end of AI.  A mid-cycle correction driven by tighter financial conditions, expensive credit, excessive leverage and a violent reset in positioning.  I’m still keeping the overall portfolio diversified across healthcare, consumer staples, utilities, Treasury exposure and other areas that are helping absorb some of the volatility.  But at the same time, I’m using this weakness to gradually increase exposure to the companies where the fundamental case remains intact.  There is one final piece worth watching.  Moves like this can become self-reinforcing once leverage starts being flushed. Forced selling creates liquidity, weak hands get flushed out and larger buyers can step in at better prices.  We’ve seen this before.  A few weeks ago, headlines around Citadel warning that further Fed tightening could trigger an economic downturn helped fuel another selloff across the AI space.  Not long after, Situational Awareness got liquidated on their positions and Citadel stepped in near the lows, taking the other side before the V-shaped reversal.  I think we may be seeing another version of that right now.  This looks a lot more like accumulation than the end of the AI cycle.

Quite a few of his observations sounded familiar.  On November 1, I published a report for JLA members explaining why I'd been reducing market exposure since early October and why I was maintaining a rather conservative stance.  My concerns went beyond the recent weakness in tech stocks.  1/ The market may be underestimating the risks heading into 2027.  The economy doesn't necessarily need to enter a recession for stocks to struggle. Slower economic and earnings growth could be enough to trigger a valuation reset when expectations are already so high.  Druckenmiller expressed a similar concern about potential economic disappointment in the second half of 2027.  2/ AI's long-term potential and the investment risks surrounding it are two different things.  I've been questioning whether the enormous capital expenditure, growing debt, and financing requirements behind AI infrastructure can continue to generate enough earnings growth to justify current expectations.  Druckenmiller also identified financing as one of the AI bearish arguments he takes seriously.  I'm still a believer in AI. That doesn't mean every AI stock is a buy at every price.  3/ The macro backdrop is becoming less forgiving.  My report highlighted persistent inflation, the risk of higher-for-longer interest rates, and the possibility that even Fed rate cuts might not be bullish if they come alongside deteriorating economic conditions.  Druckenmiller pointed to monetary tightening, weakening market breadth, widening credit spreads, and defensive stocks taking leadership.  Different indicators, but a similar message: the environment has changed, and we need to adapt.  4/  Capital preservation comes first.  I've been keeping relatively high cash levels, trading selectively, and waiting for the next genuine fat pitch rather than chasing every bounce.  Druckenmiller described his current approach as "capital preservation." His equity exposure is roughly flat, and he's not interested in forcing trades without sufficient clarity.  His exact words? "I'm not playing." So hearing him raise several similar concerns today was pretty cool, especially given how much I've learned from studying his approach over the years.  It doesn't mean we'll take the same trades or that the market will necessarily play out the way we expect.  But one of the biggest lessons I've taken from Druckenmiller is knowing when to press hard and when to step aside.  There's no prize for being fully invested all the time.  I'm happy to stay patient, protect my capital, and wait for the next fat pitch.  When the odds improve, I'll be ready to swing.

When I post about France heading toward a debt crisis, someone always replies, "But look at the US debt." Guess what, France and the United States carry comparable public debt burdens, roughly 119% of GDP for France and 127% for the US, yet the nature of that debt differs sharply.  US Treasuries sit at the center of the global financial system. They are the deepest, most liquid safe asset, the primary reserve-currency instrument, and the preferred high-quality collateral. Central banks, money-market funds, insurers, and institutional investors hold them not merely by choice but as a structural necessity for liquidity, risk management, and reserves. Flight-to-safety demand reinforces this role in stress. That captive, recurring demand gives the United States a wide margin for error.  French government bonds enjoy no such privilege. Non-residents hold a large share (around 50–60%), but this is discretionary demand driven by yield, index inclusion, and relative value within the euro area. French banks and insurers hold some for regulatory or portfolio reasons, yet nothing forces global investors to own French bonds the way the system forces them to own US Treasuries. When political or fiscal risks rise, that capital can leave quickly.  This distinction matters because France has shown little to none willingness to address the underlying drivers of its debt path. Successive governments have struggled with pension costs, and the two presidential candidates currently leading most polls, Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, both campaign on reversing the recent rise in the retirement age and returning it toward 60–62.  Markets have so far more or less tolerated this, helped by the European Central Bank’s residual presence, but tolerance is not structural. Unlike the United States, France cannot rely on a permanent global bid for its paper. If deficits remain elevated and reform stalls, spreads will eventually widen even further, funding costs will rise, and the adjustment will be imposed from outside, through higher borrowing rates, forced spending restraint, or both, rather than chosen at home.   The arithmetic is not especially subtle, only the timing is uncertain. The second Euro crisis will begin in France, and it will take down the entire Eurozone with it. In December 1941, Japanese troops captured an American surgical nurse in the Philippines.  Colonel Ruby Bradley, United States Army Nurse Corps.  For the next 37 months, she ran an operating room inside a prison camp while starving alongside her patients.  Her name was Ruby Bradley.  Born in West Virginia in 1907, she taught school before joining the United States Army Nurse Corps in 1934.  In 1943, the Japanese Army locked her inside the Santo Tomas Internment Camp in Manila with thousands of prisoners.  Food was scarce and people were dying in the barracks every week.  Ruby refused to leave the hospital ward.  As starvation stripped the weight from her bones, her uniform hung loose on her frame.  She used the empty space under her clothes to smuggle surgical tools, soap, and medicine past armed guards into the clinic.  Whenever she saw starving children crying in the dirt, she gave them her own small food ration and went to sleep hungry.  Over three years in captivity, she assisted in 230 major surgeries and helped deliver 13 babies behind barbed wire.  The prisoners called her one of the Angels in Fatigues.  On February 3, 1945, American tanks smashed through the camp gates and set them free.  Ruby walked out weighing just 86 pounds.  Everyone expected her to go home and leave the military forever.  She refused to quit.  Then war broke out in Korea in 1950.  At age 42, Ruby volunteered for the front lines as Chief Nurse of the 171st Evacuation Hospital.  In one afternoon in November 1950, her team treated 780 wounded soldiers in the bitter cold.  Days later, 100,000 Chinese troops surrounded her hospital in Pyongyang.  With enemy artillery shelling the city, commanders told Ruby to take an early flight to safety.  She refused to board a plane while wounded men were still lying in the snow.  With shells exploding nearby, she stayed on the freezing runway and loaded every injured soldier onto transport planes first.  She was the last one out.  Seconds after she stepped onto the final plane, an enemy shell blew up the ambulance she had just left behind.  She later led 500 combat nurses across Korea and became the third woman in United States Army history to reach the rank of Colonel.  She retired in 1963 with 34 medals for bravery, died in 2002 at age 94, and was buried at Arlington National Cemetery.  Across two wars, three years in a prison camp, and an enemy siege, she never once left a patient behind.
